results.title: Exogeneity tests, incomplete models, weak identification and non-Gaussian distributions: Invariance and finite-sample distributional theory - ScienceDirect
results.content: Although research on tests for exogeneity in IV regressions is widespread, most of these studies either deal with cases where instrumental variables are strong (thus leaving out issues related to weak instruments), or focus on the asymptotic properties of exogeneity tests.2 To the best of our knowledge, there is no study on the finite-sample performance of exogeneity tests when IVs can be arbitrary weak, when the errors may follow a non-Gaussian distribution, or when the reduced form is incompletely specified. In this paper, we investigate the finite-sample properties (size and power) of exogeneity tests of the type proposed by Durbin (1954), Wu (1973), Hausman (1978), and Revankar and Hartley (1973), henceforth DWH and RH tests, allowing for : (a) the possibility of identification failure (weak instruments); (b) model errors with non-Gaussian distributions, including heavy-tailed distributions which may lack moments (such as the Cauchy distribution); and (c) incomplete reduced forms (*e.g.*, situations where important instruments are missing or left out) and arbitrary heterogeneity in the reduced forms of potentially endogenous explanatory variables.

results.title: The placebo effect: Why we should care
results.content: We need to differentiate the effects of a placebo in clinical research, where research subjects are informed that they may receive “real” or “sham” treatment from what occurs during a therapeutic intervention, where patients are told that they are receiving the appropriate therapy for their ailments, because the conditions of their expectations will differ significantly. *   ### Placebo and nocebo effects for itch and itch-related immune outcomes: A systematic review of animal and human studies. Placebo effects can be described as beneficial effects that are not due to a (pharmacologically) active treatment component, but are rather elicited by contextual cues, or by positive expectations regarding treatment outcomes (Evers et al., 2018; Tausk et al., 2013). This review systematically integrates evidence from both animal (mainly rodents) and human trials on placebo and nocebo effects in itch, itch-related symptoms and conditions of the skin and mucous membranes, and related immune outcomes (e.g., histamine).

results.title: The Placebo Effect in Clinical Trials: What to Know - Altus Clinical Research
results.content: # The Placebo Effect in Clinical Trials: What to Know. When setting up a clinical trial to determine the safety and efficacy of a new treatment, it is essential to distinguish between a placebo effect and therapeutic improvement. The problem with the placebo effect is that it can mask therapeutic outcomes in research studies. A patient may not even need to receive a placebo for the effect. ## Placebo Effect on Research. Double-blind controls ensure that neither the study patients nor the study administrators know who is receiving a placebo or the study drug. A placebo is needed to mimic the known side effects of the study drug. If a patient believes they are not receiving treatment, it may cause a negative placebo effect. Therefore, it is critical to design research to distinguish significant therapeutic outcomes from a placebo effect. Altus Research understands the importance of designing research studies that distinguish between therapeutic efficacy and the placebo effect.
